title: Transperineal prostate biopsy
subtitle: MRI targets first, then a systematic template, through the perineum

sources.title: NG131 Prostate cancer: diagnosis and management

indications: A raised PSA or abnormal examination with an MRI that shows a suspicious lesion, or a clinical decision to biopsy after MRI.
contraindications: A patient who would not want or benefit from treatment of a found cancer.
preparation: Review the MRI and mark the target(s) and their zones.
Check anticoagulants and stop or bridge per plan.
Consent: bleeding in urine, semen or from the perineum, urinary retention, infection (lower than transrectal), and the chance of missing cancer.
positioning: Lithotomy, the scrotum lifted and taped away, the perineum exposed and flat.
equipment: Transrectal ultrasound with a biplanar probe, stepper or freehand access device, biopsy gun with 18G needles, local anaesthetic with a long spinal needle, labelled pots for each core.
anatomy: Prostate zones (peripheral, transition, anterior), apex and base, urethra, rectum, seminal vesicles.
criticalSafety: Take the MRI targets before systematic cores, so blood does not hide the target.
Each core is labelled by site.
commonErrors: Missing the target by sampling only systematically.
postop: Return for fever, retention or heavy bleeding.
Results at the MDT and a clinic visit booked.

steps.emphasis: The MRI has been reviewed and the targets with their zones are marked on the plan.
Antibiotic per local policy; the transperineal route carries far less sepsis risk than transrectal.
Lithotomy with the scrotum lifted and taped away from the perineum.
Clean the perineum widely; drape with the perineum exposed.
Firm pressure on the perineal puncture sites.
Every core in its own labelled pot or cassette by site, read back.
Record the number of cores per site, the targets sampled and the follow-up date.

step.tpb.block.title: Perineal and periprostatic local anaesthetic
step.tpb.block.why: A good block lets the biopsy be done awake in clinic; the periprostatic part numbs the capsule where the needle passes.
how: Raise a skin weal at the planned entry points either side of the midline above the anus.
Under ultrasound, advance a long spinal needle and infiltrate along the track to the prostatic apex on each side.
Aspirate before each injection; wait a few minutes for the block to work.
pitfalls: Injecting into the urethra or the rectum.

step.tpb.probe.title: Ultrasound probe and access device
step.tpb.probe.why: The transrectal probe only images; the needle goes through the perineal skin. The access device keeps each pass on a planned track.
how: Insert the lubricated probe into the rectum and image the prostate in the transverse and sagittal planes.
Mount the stepper or the freehand access device so the needle path shows on the sagittal view.
Measure the prostate and note the urethra on the image.
pitfalls: Losing the urethra on the image and passing through it.

step.tpb.targeted.title: Targeted cores from the MRI lesion
step.tpb.targeted.why: The MRI lesion is the most likely site of significant cancer. Sampling it first, before bleeding blurs the view, gives the highest yield.
how: Find the MRI lesion on ultrasound (cognitive or fusion registration).
Take 3 to 5 cores through the lesion, watching the needle enter the target on the sagittal view.
Put each target's cores in a pot labelled with that target.
pitfalls: Taking the systematic cores first and then not seeing the target.

step.tpb.systematic.title: Systematic template cores
step.tpb.systematic.why: Cancers outside the MRI lesion are found by systematic sampling of each zone, from apex to base.
how: Take systematic cores from each side per the local template (for example 12 to 24 cores by zone), including the anterior zones.
Avoid the urethra by keeping the needle lateral to it on the image.
pitfalls: Skipping the anterior zones, where transrectal biopsy often misses cancer.

step.tpb.retention.title: Retention or heavy bleeding after biopsy
step.tpb.retention.why: Swelling after many cores can block a big prostate. A patient who cannot pass urine should not go home without a catheter.
how: Check the patient passes urine before discharge; scan the bladder if unsure.
If in retention, pass a urethral catheter and plan a trial without catheter.
Heavy haematuria with clots needs a three-way catheter and irrigation.
pitfalls: Discharging a patient who has not voided.
